video_title: Lawfare Daily: Trump, Kim, and the Future of Korea
transcript: You know what eventually we would like to see on the table is some discussion about security guarantees about making sure that North Korea isn't accelerating their nuclear or their missile program. It's the LawFare podcast. I'm Daniel Bman, the foreign policy editor of LawFare with Andrew Yo, who is a senior fellow and the Korea Foundation chair at the Brookings Institution Center for Asia Policy Studies. The big concern is that Trump and Kim will just kind of shut out South Koreans and then negotiate their own deal. That being said, I do think President Lee has uh he's placed some hope in Trump that that whatever negotiations, whatever diplomacy unfolds between Trump and Kim could be helpful for intercore relations as well. Today we're talking about President Trump's decision to curtail exercises with South Korea and to re-engage with negotiations with North Korea. We are here to discuss the Trump administration's I'll say changing policies towards both North and South Korea. President Trump recently announced that the United States would be reducing the scope of its military exercise with South Korea as it tries to improve relations with North Korea. We're recording on August 20th and North Korea has uh just fired 10 short range ballistic missiles adding to the uncertainty about the whole US shift. Andrew, I want to have you talk us through the very complex issues both with our ally South Korea and also with North Korea. But let's begin with a little bit of history. Trump of course tried to do outreach to North Korea in the past. It did not work so well, but he first met Kim Jong-un in 2018. Can you compare the situation today on the Korean Peninsula to the one that President Trump dealt with when he was last president? >> Sure, and thanks for having me on Lawfair, Dan. It's it's great to be here with you. Um, if we think back to the Singapore and then the Hanoi summits that took place in 2018 2019 with Trump and Kim, I mean the context is quite different. At the outset, you could say that maybe not that much has changed with the peninsula. There's still tensions between North and South Korea. Peninsula is still divided, but the geopolitical context in which the peninsula is situated, I think that's changed dramatically. And I I'll just point to three things. First, North Korea rejects unification. and it sees the two Koreas as a separate state. That wasn't the case in 2018 when North and South Korea had meetings. So, President then President Moon and Kim Jong-un had two summit meetings in 2018 in April and May before Trump met him. Of course, North Korea participated in the Kungch Olympics in South Korea. So, there was pretty robust intercore relations back then and now there's absolutely nothing. North Korea's completely rejected South Korea. I think the second difference between now and back in 2018 is that North Korea is a it's a stronger and more capable country. A big part of the story of course is its security packed with Russia and the economic, diplomatic and military benefits it's now reaping from Moscow. And that leads me to my you know third sort of difference is with China and Russia in firmly in North Korea's corner the importance of US North Korea relations for Kim has diminished. So uh he just feels that he doesn't need the United States as much as he may have back in 2018. So those are some pretty big differences when you put the Korean Peninsula in a broader geopolitical context. >> Thanks. That's a kind of great way to begin our framing. I want to shift the perspective to South Korea and how Seoul sees all this. Um, Trump has described North Korea as quote unthreatening and respectful end quote. How does Soul hear that statement? >> Yeah. So, of course, I think just your average Korean probably did a double take or they're thinking, "What the heck? You know, we thought we were friends with the United States." But I think South Korean policy makers, whether they're conservative or progressive, also probably did a double take. Some may have been shocked to hear Trump describe North Korea as unthreatening. You know, this was Trump's words that North Korea's uh unthreatening and respectful. And while the current South Korean government, I think, does seek to improve uh relations with North Korea, it's emphasized, so this is South Korean government. They've emphasized the need for deterrence. They've expressed concern about North Korea's expanding drone and missile capabilities, not to mention its growing nuclear program. I mean, yesterday Trump even mentioned that North Korea possesses 57 warheads. So, I think this was pretty surprising uh for the South Koreans to hear this that North Korea is not threatening because that's certainly not the way uh South Koreans feel about the situation. But I'll just add though that I think President Lee because he does want to see engagement with with North Korea. He, you know, he'll try to make uh lemonade out of lemons. So, it's not what he wanted to hear from maybe President Trump. He didn't want to hear the criticism about not participating in Iran. But if you can use Trump's words to try to reopen diplomacy with North Korea, I think that's what the Lee government is trying to focus on right now. I want to focus now on the more short-term immediate question of the Trump administration's declaration that the United States is going to limit it the scope of the OLI freedom shield military exercises. First of all, just how important are these exercises and kind of with that in mind, if you reduce them, what are you losing here? Yeah. So, it was the reduction of joint military exercises that precipitated this whole, you know, question about North Korea and and re-engagement between Kim and Trump. But one thing that's important to understand for those that may not be familiar with the US South Korea alliance is that it's an unusually integrated military. The two countries maintain a bational combined forces command which would coordinate US and South Korean forces in the event of a conflict with North Korea. So exercises like the Uchi freedom shield uh so that's held every every August uh annually. It's not just about thousands of troops practicing maneuvers. They're also about making sure that this complicated combined command structure can actually function under a crisis or under wartime uh conditions. So with that in place, you know, the fact that the exercises were basically cut in half. They were supposed to run between August 17th to the 27th, but now they're ending on Friday. Uh so from you know 10 11 days to to just uh 5 days. No, it means that I think the the counter track drills, the live fire drills, these things are being cut back and I think you know just stopping exercises one time maybe that's in the grand scheme of things that's not going to make a huge difference in terms of US South Korea you know interoperability their ability to maintain command and control but if this is something that's done repeatedly or if and you know Trump has talked about this during his first term about joint military exercises being a big waste of money. Now, if Trump decides not to do these exercises, you know, they do them also in the spring in March, I think that could that could have some real implications for the US and South Korean military because again, they're part of this combined forces command and they do need to they need to have these exercises to maintain readiness and deterrence posture. >> I want to kind of take President Trump's claim, you know, very seriously here. Are these provocative exercises? Like, is this something that really does change threat perceptions on the North Korean side? >> Yeah. Well, it's not that there's no truth to what Trump says, but again, if you're maybe North Korea or China or maybe uh in the US, the progressive foreign policy type, you know, where US militarism is seen as the root cause of all regional instability, then yeah, maybe you could say that these massive, you know, training exercises could be provocative. But you know I would counter that these exercises are done regularly. They're scheduled uh they're announced and they're mostly defensive in nature. So on that front you know even you know before the exercises happened USFK there was a you know they did the public affairs team did announcement explaining what the exercises were for. And yes if if you're North Korea you see this as you know geared towards them and it's it's it could be very threatening. But from the perspective of the US and its allies, you got to remember that North Korea has nuclear weapons. They threaten to use them. It's in their constitution that they that they could use them, that first use would be permitted. And you know, they they constantly are saber rattling and launching testing missiles. And so for those reasons, the US and their allies need to be prepared. They need to be ready. And that's why we have these exercises. So again, it's not that there's no truth in what Trump says, but you have to remember why we have these exercises in the first place. It's to deter North Korea and defend our allies and our frankly our own strategic interests as well. >> So one thing that has changed on the North Korean side is that it has gained real battlefield experience in Ukraine. And this has involved, you know, bearing the full brunt of modern warfare, a battlefield with extensive drone use. How much should that change how the United States and South Korea plan? >> Yeah. So, North Korean forces have gained something, I think, that they didn't have before, which is real exposure to a modern drone saturated battlefield. And I I remember watching this video online where these drones were these Ukrainian drones were chasing North Korean soldiers. It was like when they were first North Koreans were first on the Russia, you know, Ukraine front and the Kurk and they were chasing these soldiers. The soldiers were scrambling and running away. And then there was one drone camera that had a close-up shot of a North Korean soldier's face. And it it was a look of confusion plus terror like all at once. and then the screen goes blank. And you know, this is the sort of warfare that the North Koreans were just thrown into. But at this point, you know, they've they've kind of figured out and now they're adapting, you know, drone technology into their own capabilities. Like they understand logistics, they understand dispersion, and this is going to help, I think, North Korea's military in the long in the long run. And so for the US South Korea alliance, I think the implications going back to you know the point about having joint military exercises that they need to also adapt and prepare because the North Koreans made uh you know it's not just that they might fire missiles uh aimed at Seoul but they might you know launch a drone attack which and they have before. There have actually been uh North Korean drones that have uh entered South Korean airspace actually in Seoul back in 2022. So there's real learning that's taking place among the North Koreans. It's not just about the the weapons and the capabilities, but it's also shifts in doctrine and the way they're incorporating these new technologies. Let's shift over to the negotiations question which is if as President Trump has announced uh there are negotiations between the two leaders and if Trump and Kim sat down tomorrow um what would they actually be negotiating about? What's on the table? >> Sure. Well, I you know, we've seen Trump meet other world leaders that you know, such as she or Putin, and I'm not sure if there would actually be any negotiating, if it would be more of just an initial meet and greet again. But you know what eventually we would like to see on the table is some discussion about security guarantees about making sure that North Korea isn't accelerating their nuclear or their missile program for that matter. So you know I I think there needs to be that sort of discussion. But what I fear is that that the security issues, the hard kind of political issues aren't really going to be addressed and instead Trump will gravitate to what he feels is more comfortable which is you know investment deals you know things or looking probably investing in North Korea for crit uh looking at North Korean critical minerals or you know developing the eastern coast of North Korea where Kim Jong has built a huge seaside resort. So I feel like those things may come up more on the economic side even though I think some of these security issues um such as you know North Korea's nuclear program the missile program particular I think those are what we want to see wi within the discussion but you know in the in the first meeting you know I think it's going to be more a meet and greet before any kind of substance is is nailed down. >> It's interesting to me that you said the substance would largely be about trying to, you know, limit the nuclear and missile programs. You know, for decades the US goal was, you know, either preventing a North Korean nuclear program or reversing it. Is that done with? Is that another era where uh the world has reluctantly accepted that North Korea is a permanent nuclear weapons state? >> Yeah. Well, I think we have to distinguish between denuclearization as a long-term objective and maybe denuclearization as a starting point for negotiations. you know, your colleague at Georgetown and CSI's Victor Chai, you know, he wrote this piece in foreign affairs, you know, the cold piece has gotten a ton of attention because it it's almost seen as an admission in South Korea that even Washington has, you know, turned to a new chapter saying that it's no longer about denuclearization, but we have to look at North Korea realistically. But I don't think it means abandoning or the denuclearization as a goal. you know, we shouldn't just simply recognize North Korea as a legitimate nuclear weapons state and then move on because that has serious implications for South Korea has implications for the non-prololiferation regime and potentially for other countries in the region as well too. So, you know, I think the consensus that seems to be uh emerging in at least in DC is that the objective should be the media objective should be threat reductions, uh arms control limitation in terms of where North Korea's uh nuclear program is at. Um so we should be asking questions like can you get a verifiable freeze on fizzle material production or can you constrain nuclear and missile testing or further expansion of its nuclear arsenal or can you introduce risk reduction measures that lower the possibility of escalation. So these are the sorts of questions they would want to see raised. And so you don't have to bring up denuclearization, you know, upfront. But my concern is, is that enough for Kim Jong-un? because when he says we don't, you know, we're done talking about denuclearization and we're keeping our nuclear stockpile uh full stop, you know, there's not a whole lot more I think the US can do or offer at that point because for us and for South Koreans and our allies, the nuclear weapons program is a serious concern. Let's shift back to South Korea and on the assumption that these negotiations go forward, but they go forward as you suggest where it's, you know, photo op. It's some discussions about economic opportunity, but it's not anything that is, you know, kind of deeply substantive on a security front. How much should we worry about the South Korean reaction to this? How does this affect the bilateral relationship? >> Yeah. So what South Korea is often fearful of is this there's this term called South Korea passen meaning that Trump and Kim are going to negotiate and then Trump is going to completely forget about what South Korea's interests are in this diplomatic engagement and you know one good example is you know I I mentioned this artillery North Korean artillery is all aimed towards soul and so a big concern is short range ballistic missiles but if Trump says that well the real threat is North Korea's intercontinental ballistic missiles. And so they want to they want to freeze, you know, testing ICBM testing, but they don't say anything about the short-range missiles. That would be problematic for South Korea. But but that is the the big concern is that Trump and Kim will just kind of shut out South Koreans and then negotiate their own deal. That being said, I do think President Lee has uh he's placed some hope in Trump that that whatever negotiations, whatever diplomacy unfolds between Trump and Kim could be helpful for inter Korea relations as well. as you and maybe some of the listeners know, North Korea, as I said up at the top, has completely rejected uh South Korea in terms of like South Korean overtures for engagement, for aid, for assistance. And I think Lee is hoping to perhaps ride on the coattails of Trump if he's able to engage with Kim that that Trump would do him a solid and also encourage him to reach out to South South Korea as well. So that I when I said that Lee is trying to make lemonade out of lemons with Trump's, you know, latest truth social post. I really do think that he is trying to he's hoping that some door can open towards uh diplomacy or at least some environment for uh diplomatic dialogue can be created through a a Kim Trump meeting. I want to step back beyond the I'll say current situation and just ask more broadly what do you think Americans and this can be you know people who follow the issue generally or experts but what do you think Americans kind of systematically misunderstand about North Korea today? So for those that don't follow North Korea repeatedly, our image of North Korea is it's this, you know, isolated pariah state that's extremely poor but has lots of nuclear weapons. That's still correct. But there have been a series of articles in the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times, uh, Washington Post about just how much North Korean society is changing that, you know, Americans will be shocked to know that they have mobile banking, you know, online banking, mobile pay, there's some like Uberlike, you know, service. And so if if you just looked at the photos or if you just looked at North Korea propaganda, you would think this looks like, you know, Hong Kong or Shanghai. Obviously this is just the capital and it's not they're large parts of the country they're extremely poor but North Korea has move forged ahead despite sanctions despite its isolation from the west they've been able to uh move forward and this is accelerated with support from Russia uh and China. So I think for most Americans I think they would be surprised to see you know how you know technologically savvy the North Koreans have become. I mean those are they're in the I mean you might follow this a little bit Dan but you know North Korea is one of the worst actors out there when it comes to to cyber heists and in terms of you know cryp they're big into cryptocurrency and crypto theft. I think $2 billion were stolen by my North Korean actors you know between 2022 and 2024. So that's something that I think Americans may need to update that North Korea is not so isolated as it once was and it's not I mean it's not this poor backward country that we we may have been thinking for for decades. So that's that's something that we we do need to update. I guess uh folks like myself or or Victor over at CSIS need to make that point clear. That's a different North Korea from what it was 10 or 20 years ago. >> Excellent. That's fascinating. Let me again flip to South Korea. Is there a fear or concern that South Korea has that you feel is not sufficiently appreciated in Washington circles? >> I I mean, so there's always this question about whether South Koreans are hedging between China and between China and the United States. I'm sure we're going to hear some of this in the next week or so. Wangi was actually in uh Soul today, you know, holding meetings with South Korea's national security advisor. And so, you know, folks in know in the Trump administration may again be asking why is why are the South Koreans talking to the to the Chinese? But I think something that Washington maybe doesn't sufficiently appreciate is that the Korean Peninsula is on the border with China. And this isn't just an issue. It's not just a hard, you know, security issue for the South Koreans. I think for South Koreans who still think about unification that think about intercore relations, it's it's yeah, it's not just about security, but it's an issue that relates to unification. For that reason, the Koreans, they like to there's this framing where they say it's either alliance or autonomy. That you either choose the alliance or you want to kind of go your own way and you want to choose autonomy. I this is one of the reasons why South Koreans are spending much more in the defense that they want to uh make sure that they're properly equipped if you know the US moves in a different direction and but I think most Koreans even the progressive uh elite government they'll say that it's not really a choice for us but it's really you know alliance and autonomy and it's because of this strategic neighborhood that they live in that they have China at their border that they're you know they feel in their history they've always and they've been undercut by great power politics whether it's at the start of the cold war when the peninsula was divided or when it was in the late 19th century when Japan, China uh and Russia were vying for control in the Korean peninsula. And I think that has an impact on the way South Koreans think about their security and their security environment. And so when it comes to things like North Korea, when it comes to, you know, its relationship with China, they feel that there's this historical, I guess, narrative, if you will, that it kind of shapes their thinking about their environment. And so that's something that I think sometimes uh folks in Washington don't really get. And it's it's kind of hard to explain. There's a lot of context and nuance behind it, but someone like President Trump, he doesn't really do nuance. So yeah, but that's something that I think South Koreans think so uh you know Washington doesn't sufficiently appreciate. >> Most of what we've talked about has been on, you know, military exercises or negotiations, but a a relatively short-term set of questions focused on the coming months. Let's fast forward 5 years. It's a different administration and we're looking at North Korea. What would constitute a successful US policy towards North Korea in those five years where you'd feel five years from now, hey, that actually went reasonably well? >> Sure. I mean, it depends how high or how low you set set the bar. I mean, five years ago from now is was it's like 2021. I mean, there's nothing going on. The last US North Korea official engagement was in October October of 2019. It took place in Stockholm, Sweden. Since then there's been zero engagement. There's been no intercore engagement. You know, it's it's a pretty low bar if if you say just having some diplomatic engagement would be a success. But that's how difficult this North Korea problem has been. That it certainly for sure it hasn't gotten better. If anything, it's gotten worse because North Korea's capabilities continues to grow. So if you can at least get North Korea to put a hold or put a freeze that's verifiable on their nuclear program and have some diplomatic engagement between US and North Korea or even among uh the parties you know South Korea is talking about this four they're talking again about a four-party you know discussion between Beijing Pyongyang Soul and Washington if there's some dialogue that's taking place uh without North Korea moving further on its nuclear program I think that would be a huge huge success compared to what we've seen in the previous 5 years. >> That strikes me as a a realistic benchmark for success. And I'm going to end on that optimistic note that maybe we can, you know, if we can't move forward, at least we can avoid moving farther backwards. >> Well, it's rare to get hear the word optimism and North Korea policy in the same sentence. So, I'm I'm glad you're ending on that note, Dan. Uh maybe I should say a less pessimistic than usual. >> Andrew Yo, thank you very much for joining us. >> Thanks for having me here. >> You can get adfree versions of this and other lawfare podcasts by becoming a lawfare material supporter at our website lawfare media.org/support. You'll also get access to special events and other content available only to our supporters. Please rate and review us wherever you get your podcasts. Look out for other podcasts including Rational Security, Allies, the Aftermath, and Escalation, our latest LawFare Presents podcast series about the war in Ukraine. Check out our written work as well at lawfare media.org. The podcast is edited by Jen Patcha and our audio engineer this episode was Go Rodeo. Our theme song is from Alibi Music. As always, thank you for listening.
